title: The Michelangelo Phenomenon
text:
Michelangelo is often credited with the idea that a statue already lies hidden in the block of stone, and the sculptor's task is to chip away whatever hides it. Stephen Drigotas, Caryl Rusbult and their colleagues borrowed the image to describe something that happens in close relationships.

Each person has an ideal self: the person they hope to become, with the skills, traits and goals they are reaching for. A partner can help or hinder that. The researchers proposed that when a partner sees you in a way that fits your ideal, and behaves toward you in ways that draw out those qualities, you gradually move toward that ideal self. They called this partner affirmation.

In a series of four studies with dating and married couples, the team measured how each partner perceived and treated the other, using both partners' reports and, in some studies, observers' ratings, and in some cases followed couples over time. Where partners affirmed each other's ideals, people reported more movement toward their ideal selves. That growth went along with greater well-being in the relationship and a better chance of staying together.

The idea suggested that good partners do not only accept each other; they help each other grow.
lesson: Get to know who your partner, child or friend is trying to become, and treat them as that person already. Your view of them can help shape them.
people: Stephen Drigotas, Caryl Rusbult, Jennifer Wieselquist, Sarah Whitton
source: Drigotas, S. M., Rusbult, C. E., Wieselquist, J., and Whitton, S. W. (1999). Close partner as sculptor of the ideal self: Behavioral affirmation and the Michelangelo phenomenon. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(2), 293-323.
